claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn is initially a fully annealed, single-phase FCC solid solution without BCC precipitates.
The onset of yielding is dominated by thermally activated dislocation nucleation from pre-existing defects rather than by a phase transformation.
Surface steps and intrinsic stacking faults act as dislocation-nucleation sites in single-crystal FeNiCrMn.
Grain boundaries can act as dislocation-nucleation sites in polycrystalline material.
Chemical disorder and constituent-atom size or lattice-parameter differences generate high lattice friction in the FCC HEA.
High configurational entropy produces severe lattice distortion and increases the Peierls stress.
The elevated lattice-friction barrier makes yield strength anomalously insensitive to strain rate.
A small activation volume for dislocation nucleation contributes to the low strain-rate sensitivity.
Lattice friction is relatively insensitive to thermal activation at low temperature but becomes rate-limiting at higher temperature.
FeNiCrMn has high or moderate stacking-fault energy that suppresses extensive twinning at yield relative to CoCrNi alloys.
Dislocation glide is favored over twinning as the yield mechanism.
The alloy remains FCC during deformation up to 600 K.
BCC precipitation requires specific thermal histories such as long-term aging that are absent during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
The strain-rate sensitivity exponent will remain below 0.05 from 77 K to 600 K over strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1.
Dislocation glide will occur on FCC {111} planes.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation will occur at strains below 5%.
Yield anisotropy follows FCC Schmid-factor-dependent slip activation, with [001] loading producing a lower yield strength than [111] loading because of multiple active slip systems.
Traditional FCC metals such as Cu and Ni have higher strain-rate sensitivity and lower cryogenic yield strength than HEAs.
Above 600 K, creep or phase precipitation may become relevant, so the proposed mechanism is not asserted in that regime.
A strain-rate sensitivity exponent above 0.1 indicates strong thermal activation typical of phase transformations or diffusion.
